decisionMemo.businessProblem: A regional homebuilder generating $1.2B in home closing revenue committed land, lots, and a construction pipeline sized for a higher-volume forecast, but demand has softened: net new orders fell to 2,150 against 2,400 homes closed (orders now below closings, so backlog is shrinking), absorption dropped from 3.2 to 2.4 homes per community per month, and the cancellation rate rose from 14% to 22%. As a result, unsold spec inventory has built to 620 homes versus a normal level near 380, and the owned-and-optioned land pipeline stands at ~9,000 lots (about 3.75 years of supply at the current pace). Margin pressure is compounding: homebuilding gross margin fell 400 bps (22% to 18%) as land cost per home rose 15% (to $150k) and labor rose 9%, while market softness caps price and forces incentives up to ~3% of ASP ($15k/home). The core question: is this a volume/demand-to-supply commitment problem (the company built and optioned ahead of demand that did not materialize), a unit-cost problem (land and labor inflation eroding margin), or a pricing-structure problem (mispriced relative to the market)? The owner must decide within ~90 days, before the next land-bank funding cycle and board meeting, whether to slow starts, walk option lots (forfeiting deposits), or raise incentives, while capital is increasingly locked in spec and land.
